title: Numbers and time
seoTitle: Turkmen numbers, telling the time and dates
intro: This unit is about counting: the numbers up to the millions, the singular noun that follows them (*iki kitap*, two books), the ordinals (*birinji*, first), the clock, the calendar, and how to give your age and a price. Most of it rests on endings you know: the locative says **at** a time (*sagat bäşde*), the genitive builds the half hour, and the possessive with the locative gives your age (*ýigrimi ýaşymda*).

blocks.text: You know *bir*, *iki* and *üç*. Here are the rest of the building blocks. *üç* (3) and *dört* (4) have a long vowel, which is why *dört* softens before a vowel: *dördünji* (fourth). Zero is *nol*.

Bigger numbers are built the way they are said in English, from the largest part down, and **each part is a separate word**: 11 is *on bir* (ten one), 25 *ýigrimi bäş*, 150 *ýüz elli*, 2026 *iki müň ýigrimi alty*. Hundreds and thousands are counted in front: *iki ýüz* (200), *bäş müň* (5,000). A million is *million*: *bir million* (1,000,000).
Numbers are often written in digits. A suffix after a digit follows the number as it is said and comes after a hyphen: *5-e* (to five), *10-dan* (from ten), *2026-njy* (2026th).

blocks.title: Seven or seventy?
blocks.text: *ýedi* (7) and *ýetmiş* (70), *alty* (6) and *altmyş* (60), *sekiz* (8) and *segsen* (80) look alike. The tens end in *-myş*, *-miş* or *-sen*, *-san*: *altmyş*, *ýetmiş*, *segsen*, *togsan*.

sections.title: Two book: the singular after numbers

blocks.text: After a number the noun stays **singular**: *iki kitap* (two books), *on okuwçy* (ten pupils), never *iki kitaplar*. The number already says there is more than one. The same goes for words of quantity: *köp* (many), *az* (few), *birnäçe* (several) and the question *näçe?* (how many?).

items.en: There are twenty pupils in the class.
I have two brothers or sisters.
There are few people here.
There are a few people in the shop.
There are three apples on the table.

blocks.text: **sany and kişi.** When you count things, Turkmen often puts *sany* (piece) between the number and the noun: *üç sany alma*, three apples. It adds nothing to the meaning, and you can leave it out. People are counted with *kişi* (person) or *adam*: *bäş kişi*, five people. Ask *Näçe kişi?*, how many people?

blocks.title: No plural after a number
blocks.text: *iki kitaplar*, *bäş adamlar*, *köp dükanlar* are wrong. Say *iki kitap*, *bäş adam*, *köp dükan*.

Add `-(Y)njY` to a number to make **first, second, third**: *-ynjy* or *-inji* after a consonant, just *-njy* or *-nji* after a vowel, with the vowel rounding after *o, ö, u, ü* in the first syllable. In a compound number only the last word takes it: *ýigrimi bäşinji*, twenty-fifth.

With digits, write a hyphen and *-njy* or *-nji*, by the last vowel of the number as it is said: *6-njy* (*altynjy*), *9-njy* (*dokuzynjy*), *27-nji* (*ýigrimi ýedinji*), *1991-nji* (*… togsan birinji*), *2026-njy* (*… ýigrimi altynjy*). The ordinal comes before its noun: *ikinji gün*, the second day; *üçünji sapak*, the third lesson.

items.en: Monday is the first day of the week.
This is my third lesson.
Our room is on the second floor.
This year is 2026.

sections.title: What time is it? Sagat näçe?

blocks.text: Ask *Sagat näçe?*, literally **the clock is how much?** Answer with *sagat* and the hour: *Sagat bäş*, it's five. To say **at** a time, put the locative on the number: *sagat bäşde*, at five. So **at what time?** is *Sagat näçede?*, or just *Näçede?*

items.en: What time is it? — It's nine o'clock.
The lesson starts at nine.
I get up at seven in the morning.
What time are you coming?

blocks.text: There is no **a.m.** and **p.m.**: say the part of the day first, *irden* (in the morning), *günortan* (at noon), *öýlän* (in the afternoon), *agşam* (in the evening), *gije* (at night): *agşam sagat sekizde*, at eight in the evening. Timetables and the news use the 24-hour clock in digits.

**Half past.** Turkmen counts toward the coming hour. 4:30 is **the half of five**: the coming hour in the genitive, then *ýary*, **its half**. (*ýarym* on its own is **half**: *ýarym sagat*, half an hour.) **At** half past four is *bäşiň ýarynda*, with the *n* of [A1 unit 10](a1-u10) before the locative.

After a vowel the genitive is *-nyň, -niň* in writing (*ikiniň*, *altynyň*, *ýediniň*); in speech you will often hear the short *ikiň*, *altyň*, *ýediň*. This course writes the long form and accepts both.

**Minutes to the hour** also look ahead: the coming hour in the dative, then the minutes, then *bar* (there are): *Bäşe on minut bar*, it's ten to five (literally **to five there are ten minutes**). A quarter is simply *on bäş minut*: *Alta on bäş minut bar*, it's a quarter to six.

blocks.title: bäşiň ýary is 4:30
blocks.text: *bäşiň ýary* is not 5:30 but 4:30, half of the way to five. In the same way *Bäşe on minut bar* is 4:50. Find the coming hour first, then count back.

blocks.title: Minutes past the hour
blocks.text: In speech, minutes past the hour count from the coming hour too, with the verb *işlemek*: *Altydan on minut işleýär*, it's ten past five (literally **ten minutes have run from six**). In writing, schedules simply use digits with the suffix after a hyphen: *sagat 8:20-de*, at 8:20; *agşam sagat 20:30-da*.
The days of the week and the months are written with a small letter, in a date too. Monday comes first; ask *Şu gün haýsy gün?*, what day is it today? **On Monday** is *duşenbe güni*.

A date is the **ordinal** and the month: *27-nji oktýabr*, 27 October. **On** a date takes the locative: *27-nji oktýabrda*. **In** a month or a year likewise: *martda* (in March), *2026-njy ýylda* (in 2026). A full date puts the year first, in the genitive, and the month with **its**: *2026-njy ýylyň 13-nji noýabry*, 13 November 2026.

items.en: Today is Friday.
Nowruz is on 21 March.
My birthday is on 12 October.
I don't work on Sunday.
There are seven days in a week.

blocks.text: The seasons are *ýaz* (spring), *tomus* (summer), *güýz* (autumn) and *gyş* (winter). *ýaz* has a long vowel; with a short one, *ýaz!* is **write!**, from *ýazmak*.

blocks.title: The date needs its ordinal
blocks.text: In a date the day is an ordinal: write *12-nji oktýabr* (*on ikinji oktýabr*), not *12 oktýabr*, and keep the month in lowercase.

**Age** uses *ýaş* (age) with a possessive and the locative, literally **I am at my twenty years**: *Men ýigrimi ýaşymda*. Ask *Sen näçe ýaşyňda?* or, politely, *Siz näçe ýaşyňyzda?* For anyone else, *ýaşynda*, with the *n*: *Kakam elli ýaşynda*, my father is fifty.

**Prices** are in manat, and a manat has a hundred *teňňe*: *iki manat elli teňňe*, 2.50 manat. Ask *Bu näçe manat?* or *Bahasy näçe?* ([A1 unit 8](a1-u08)). At the market you will also hear *Näçeden?*, how much each, or a kilo.

items.tk: Sen näçe ýaşyňda? — Men ýigrimi alty ýaşymda.
items.seg: Sen näçe ýaş|yň|da? — Men ýigrimi alty ýaş|ym|da.
items.en: How old are you? — I'm twenty-six.
How old is your mother?
This book is forty manats.
The bread is two manats fifty.
There are a hundred tenge in a manat.

blocks.title: The pronoun can go
blocks.text: The ending of *ýaşymda* already says **my**, so *Ýigrimi ýaşymda* is enough. As everywhere, after a number *manat* and *ýaş* stay singular.

summary: Numbers are built from the largest part down, as separate words: *ýigrimi bäş*, *iki müň ýigrimi alty*. After a number or *köp, az, birnäçe, näçe* the noun stays singular: *iki kitap*. Things can take *sany*; people are counted with *kişi*.
Ordinals add `-(Y)njY`: *birinji, ikinji, üçünji, dördünji, altynjy*; with digits *5-nji*, *6-njy*, *2026-njy*.
*Sagat näçe? — Sagat bäş.* **At** a time: *sagat bäşde*; the part of the day goes first: *agşam sagat sekizde*.
Half hours and minutes to count toward the coming hour: *bäşiň ýary* (4:30), *bäşiň ýarynda* (at 4:30), *Bäşe on minut bar* (4:50).
Days and months in lowercase; dates with the ordinal: *27-nji oktýabrda*; *duşenbe güni*, on Monday.
Age: *Sen näçe ýaşyňda? — Men ýigrimi ýaşymda.* Prices: *iki manat elli teňňe*; a manat has 100 *teňňe*.
